```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 144, out.width = "100%", dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

This article draws familiar charts and solid geometry from small datasets. Each example gives the data and the code that draws it. [Layers](layers.html) explains the data layers, and [Vector fields](vector-fields.html) develops the streamtube example. Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html).

## Domain recipes

[Tensor glyphs](tensors.html) draw symmetric tensors as ellipsoids or superquadrics. [Ordination biplots](ordination.html) combine site scores, variable arrows and group regions. [Molecular views](molecules.html) draw atoms and bonds from bio3d records. [Colour gamuts](colour-gamuts.html) place sampled colours and their convex hull in Lab coordinates.

## Parametric curves

Sample a curve in row order and sweep a circular cross-section along it to
give it thickness. The trefoil knot below is traced by three sine and cosine
terms in a parameter `t` from 0 to 2&pi;. The closed tube joins its last
cross-section to its first.

```{r knot, fig.alt="A solid blue trefoil tube crossing over and under itself three times."}
t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 121)[-121]
knot <- data.frame(x = sin(t) + 2 * sin(2 * t),
                   y = cos(t) - 2 * cos(2 * t),
                   z = -sin(3 * t))
ggplot(knot, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_tube_3d(radius = 0.16, sides = 10, closed = TRUE, fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

At each of the three crossings, the strand nearer the camera is drawn over the other. [Layers](layers.html#tubes-ribbons-and-sweeps) shows ribbons and custom cross-sections along curves.

## Solid violins

The iris data record flower measurements in centimetres for three species.
Revolve each species' estimated petal-length density around a vertical
axis. The width changes along that axis with the density, giving each
species a solid violin.

```{r solid-violins, fig.alt="Three revolved petal-length violins for the iris species, separated along x."}
ggplot(iris, aes(Species, y = 0, z = Petal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_violin_3d(shape = "revolve", n = 40, sides = 16) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), breaks = NULL, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "teal")])) +
  coord_3d(elevation = 20)
```

## Covariance ellipsoids

Three measurements place each iris flower in space. Estimate a normal
covariance ellipsoid for each species to show the direction and extent
of its spread. Translucent faces reveal the points and principal axes.

```{r covariance, fig.alt="Three translucent covariance ellipsoids around iris measurements, with points and principal axes visible."}
ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, z = Petal.Length,
                 colour = Species, fill = Species)) +
  stat_ellipsoid_3d(type = "norm", kind = "data", alpha = 0.2,
                     axes = TRUE, detail = 2) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "teal")])) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "teal")])) +
  coord_3d(azimuth = -45, elevation = 25)
```

The data ellipsoids describe variation among flowers. Confidence ellipsoids
for the species means use the standard-error kind, as shown in
[Layers](layers.html#spheres-ellipsoids-and-glyphs).

## Streamtubes

A rotating vector field with a positive vertical component produces rising
helices. Integrate from three seeds at different radii, then give each
curve a circular cross-section. Fill represents the vector magnitude along
each tube.

```{r streamtubes, fig.alt="Three rising helical streamtubes in a rotating vector field, coloured by vector magnitude."}
field <- expand.grid(x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 5),
                     y = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 5), z = c(-1, 0, 1))
field <- transform(field, u = -y, v = x, w = 0.2)
seeds <- rbind(c(0.3, 0, -0.8), c(0.55, 0, -0.8), c(0.8, 0, -0.8))
ggplot(field, aes(x, y, z = z, u = u, v = v, w = w)) +
  stat_streamline_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(norm)), seeds = seeds,
    geom = "tube", direction = "forward", step = 0.1, max_steps = 80,
    radius = 0.035, sides = 8, cap = "flat", colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = PAL["blue"], high = PAL["orange"]) +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

## A capped cutaway

Subtract a smaller sphere from a larger one to make a hollow shell. A
clipping plane removes the half at positive x. Capping closes the cut
with an annulus and preserves the inner cavity.

```{r cutaway, fig.alt="A hollow sphere cut in half, with an annular cap around its visible inner cavity."}
shell <- sdf_sphere(radius = 1) - sdf_sphere(radius = 0.65)
ggplot() + geom_isofunction_3d(fun = shell, n = 24, fill = PAL["teal"]) +
  xlim(-1.1, 1.1) + ylim(-1.1, 1.1) + zlim(-1.1, 1.1) +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data", azimuth = -30,
    clip_planes = list(clip_plane_3d(c(-1, 0, 0), c(x = 0), cap = TRUE)))
```

[Implicit surfaces](implicit-surfaces.html) shows how to construct shapes
from functions and reconstruct them from point samples.

## Functions of two variables

`geom_function()` draws a function of x as a line. `geom_function_3d()` samples a function of x and y on a grid and draws the result as a surface. The x and y limits set the sampling range, and `n` sets the number of grid points along each axis. The function below is the radial sinc, sin(r)/r, where r is the distance from the origin.

```{r sinc, fig.alt="A surface with a central peak of height one surrounded by concentric ripples, shaded from light to dark blue with height."}
sinc <- function(x, y) {
  r <- sqrt(x^2 + y^2)
  sin(r) / r
}
ggplot() +
  geom_function_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(z_mean)), fun = sinc, n = 40) +
  xlim(-10, 10) + ylim(-10, 10) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEAF3", high = PAL["blue"]) +
  coord_3d()
```

The fill maps `z_mean`, the mean height of each triangle, so the ripples are distinguished by shade as well as by position.

## Bézier curves

A cubic Bézier curve is defined by four control points P0 to P3. For a parameter s from 0 to 1, the curve passes through (1 - s)^3 P0 + 3s(1 - s)^2 P1 + 3s^2(1 - s) P2 + s^3 P3. It starts at P0 and ends at P3; P1 and P2 pull it towards them without lying on it. Write the four weights as columns of a matrix and multiply by the control points to get the sampled curve.

```{r bezier-data}
ctrl <- data.frame(x = c(0, 1, 3, 4), y = c(0, 3, -1, 2),
                   z = c(0, 3, 3, 0))
s <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 100)
weights <- cbind((1 - s)^3, 3 * s * (1 - s)^2, 3 * s^2 * (1 - s), s^3)
bezier <- as.data.frame(weights %*% as.matrix(ctrl))
head(bezier, 3)
```

In two dimensions the sampled points would go to `geom_path()`. Here the curve is a `geom_path_3d()` layer, and the control polygon is a dashed path through the control points.

```{r bezier, fig.alt="A blue cubic Bezier curve rising from the first control point and returning to the floor at the fourth, with a dashed grey control polygon joining the four grey control points."}
ggplot(bezier, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_path_3d(data = ctrl, linetype = "dashed", colour = PAL["grey"]) +
  geom_point_3d(data = ctrl, size = 3, colour = PAL["grey"]) +
  geom_path_3d(linewidth = 1.2, colour = PAL["blue"]) +
  coord_3d()
```

The curve touches the polygon only at its two end points, and it leaves each end along the polygon's first and last edge.

## Bivariate histograms

`geom_bin_2d()` counts observations in rectangular cells of two continuous variables and shows each count as a fill colour. In three dimensions the count becomes the height of a column. The `faithful` data record the duration of 272 eruptions of the Old Faithful geyser and the waiting time before each, both in minutes. `geom_histogram_3d()` assigns each eruption to a cell 0.5 minutes wide in duration and 5 minutes wide in waiting time, counts the eruptions in each cell and draws one column per occupied cell; neighbouring columns touch, as histogram bars do.

```{r hist, fig.alt="Columns counting Old Faithful eruptions by duration and waiting time, forming two clusters: short eruptions after short waits and long eruptions after long waits."}
ggplot(faithful, aes(eruptions, waiting)) +
  geom_histogram_3d(binwidth = c(0.5, 5), fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  labs(x = "duration", z = "count") +
  coord_3d()
```

The two clusters are the short eruptions after waits of about 50 minutes and the long eruptions after waits of about 80 minutes.

## Grouped bar charts

`geom_col(position = "dodge")` places the bars of a second grouping variable side by side within each x category. In three dimensions the second variable takes the y axis. Compute the median price of the diamonds in each combination of cut grade and four of the seven colour grades, from D (colourless) to J.

```{r grouped-data}
some_colours <- subset(diamonds, color %in% c("D", "F", "H", "J"))
some_colours$color <- droplevels(some_colours$color)
prices <- aggregate(price ~ cut + color, data = some_colours,
                    FUN = median)
head(prices, 3)
```

Both factors map to position directly, and the median price maps to z. The x axis has room for only some of the five cut names, so the fill repeats the cut grade with a legend.

```{r grouped, fig.alt="Columns of median diamond price by cut grade along x and colour grade along y; for the Very Good, Premium and Ideal cuts the price rises from colour D to colour J."}
ggplot(prices, aes(cut, color, z = price, fill = cut)) +
  geom_col_3d() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[1:5])) +
  coord_3d() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

For the Very Good, Premium and Ideal cuts, the median price rises from colour D to colour J. The Fair and Good cuts have a higher median at D than at F.

## Pie charts

A ggplot2 pie chart is a stacked bar in `coord_polar(theta = "y")`. In three dimensions each slice is a wedge polygon raised to a common height with `geom_extrude_3d()`. The data give the share of each cut grade among all diamonds; each wedge spans an angle proportional to its share, sampled at 40 points on its arc.

```{r pie-data}
share <- prop.table(table(diamonds$cut))
edges <- c(0, cumsum(share)) * 2 * pi
wedges <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(share), function(i) {
  arc <- seq(edges[i], edges[i + 1], length.out = 40)
  data.frame(cut = names(share)[i], x = c(0, cos(arc)), y = c(0, sin(arc)))
}))
round(share, 2)
```

Each wedge starts at the centre and runs along its arc; `group = cut` keeps the five polygons apart. The extrusion height is a constant `z`, and the aspect flattens the disc.

```{r pie, fig.alt="A flat three-dimensional pie of five coloured wedges for the diamond cut grades; the Ideal wedge covers about two fifths of the disc and the Fair wedge the smallest sliver."}
wedges$cut <- factor(wedges$cut, levels = names(share))
ggplot(wedges, aes(x, y, z = 0.2, group = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_extrude_3d() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[1:5])) +
  coord_3d(aspect = c(1, 1, 0.2), elevation = 35, axes = character(),
           panes = character(), box = "none") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

Ideal diamonds make up 40% of the data and Fair diamonds 3%. The walls are lit by their angle to the light, so the front of the disc is darker than the top.

## Several series over time

A line chart of several series maps time to x and each series to a colour (`geom_line(aes(colour = variable))`). In three dimensions each series gets its own position on y. A wall runs from zero up to its value. `economics_long` holds monthly US economic series in long format, with `value01` rescaled to run from 0 to 1 in each series. Three of them are used here: the personal savings rate, the median duration of unemployment and the number of unemployed.

```{r series-data}
econ <- subset(economics_long,
               variable %in% c("psavert", "uempmed", "unemploy"))
econ$series <- match(econ$variable, c("psavert", "uempmed", "unemploy"))
range(econ$value01)
```

`geom_band_3d()` with `zmin` and `zmax` mapped draws a vertical wall along the x/y path of each group. The y axis labels as many series names as fit along its edge, and the legend names all three.

```{r series, fig.alt="Three walls along the date axis from 1967 to 2015, one each for the savings rate, median unemployment duration and number of unemployed, with heights rescaled to zero to one."}
ggplot(econ, aes(date, series, zmin = 0, zmax = value01,
                 group = variable, fill = variable)) +
  geom_band_3d() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:3,
                     labels = c("psavert", "uempmed", "unemploy")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "teal")])) +
  coord_3d(azimuth = -50, aspect = c(1.6, 1, 0.8)) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

Both unemployment series reach their highest values in 2009 and 2010. The savings rate falls from above 12% in the early 1970s to its lowest value in 2005.

## Scatter plots with a fitted surface

`geom_smooth()` fits y as a function of x and draws the fitted line over the points. `geom_smooth_3d()` fits z as a function of x and y and draws the fitted surface. Here the `mtcars` fuel consumption (`mpg`, miles per gallon) is modelled by weight (`wt`, in 1,000 lb) and gross horsepower (`hp`). The formula uses the names x, y and z for the mapped variables and adds a quadratic term in weight.

```{r smooth, fig.alt="A dark blue fitted surface of miles per gallon against weight and horsepower, curving down with weight, between two pale confidence surfaces, with red points for the 32 cars."}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, hp, z = mpg)) +
  geom_smooth_3d(method = "lm", formula = z ~ x + I(x^2) + y,
                 n = 20, fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 2.5, colour = PAL["red"]) +
  coord_3d()
```

The pale surfaces above and below the fit are the pointwise 95% confidence bounds for the mean, the counterpart of the grey ribbon around `geom_smooth()`. Points below the fitted surface are hidden by it.

## Two-dimensional densities

`geom_density_2d()` draws contour lines of a bivariate kernel density estimate. `stat_density_2d_3d()` computes the same kind of estimate and draws the density as height. The sample below holds 2,000 diamonds under 2.5 carats, with price on a log10 scale.

```{r density, fig.alt="A density surface over carat and log10 price, with its highest peak just above 0.3 carats and smaller peaks near 0.7, 1 and 1.5 carats, shaded by density."}
set.seed(1)
small <- subset(diamonds, carat < 2.5)
small <- small[sample(nrow(small), 2000), ]
ggplot(small, aes(carat, log10(price))) +
  stat_density_2d_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(density)), n = 40) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEAF3", high = PAL["blue"]) +
  coord_3d()
```

The peaks follow a ridge that rises in price with carat. They sit just above 0.3, 0.7, 1 and 1.5 carats, where the sample holds more stones than at neighbouring weights.

## Contour lines

`geom_contour()` draws the lines where a gridded height crosses a set of levels. `geom_contour_3d()` draws the same lines on the surface, each at the height of its level. `volcano` holds heights in metres of Maunga Whau on a 10 m grid, 87 rows by 61 columns.

```{r contour-data}
heights <- data.frame(x = rep(seq_len(nrow(volcano)), ncol(volcano)),
                      y = rep(seq_len(ncol(volcano)), each = nrow(volcano)),
                      z = as.vector(volcano))
range(heights$z)
```

A grey surface carries the lines, drawn every 10 m and coloured by level.

```{r contour, fig.alt="A grey surface of the Maunga Whau volcano with contour lines every ten metres, coloured from blue at 100 metres to red at 190 metres, ringing the crater."}
ggplot(heights, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey80", colour = NA) +
  geom_contour_3d(aes(colour = after_stat(level)), binwidth = 10,
                  linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = PAL["blue"], high = PAL["red"]) +
  coord_3d(azimuth = -40, elevation = 40, aspect = c(1.4, 1, 0.6))
```

The lines close round the summit and the crater rim. Lines on the far slope are hidden where the near slope covers them. ggplot2's own `geom_contour()` also works inside `coord_3d()`, drawing each line at its level without the surface.

## Filled contour terraces

ggplot2's filled contour layer divides the volcano heights into bands.
Adding the 3D coordinate system raises each band to its level midpoint,
producing horizontal terraces with the original band colours.

```{r filled-terraces, fig.alt="The volcano's filled contour bands lifted into coloured terraces, with the crater opening retained."}
ggplot(heights, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_contour_filled(bins = 6, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[1:6])) +
  coord_3d(azimuth = -40, elevation = 40, aspect = c(1.4, 1, 0.6))
```

[Combining 2D and 3D graphics](combining-2d-3d.html) shows terraced bands
and contour maps placed on the floor below a surface.
